learn.intro: After 1945 Americans feared communism abroad and spies at home. Senator Joseph McCarthy exploited that fear — until television helped bring him down.

blocks.p: The Cold War, 1945–50: the USSR took control of Eastern Europe; the Berlin Blockade (1948–49) raised tension; in 1949 the USSR tested an atomic bomb and China became communist; in June 1950 the Korean War began. Many Americans felt communism was spreading and feared enemies inside the USA.

Spy cases seemed to prove the danger. Alger Hiss, a former State Department official, was accused in 1948 of spying for the USSR and convicted of perjury (lying under oath) in 1950. Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were arrested in 1950 for passing atomic secrets and executed in 1953.

Government action: President Truman's Loyalty Program (1947) investigated millions of federal employees. The FBI under J. Edgar Hoover watched suspected communists. The House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC) investigated Hollywood: in 1947 the 'Hollywood Ten' refused to answer its questions, were jailed and blacklisted.

sections.title: 2. McCarthy's methods and the growth of opposition

blocks.p: On 9 February 1950, in a speech at Wheeling, West Virginia, Senator Joseph McCarthy claimed to have a list of 205 communists working in the State Department. He never produced proof.

His methods: making accusations without evidence, changing his numbers, smearing opponents as 'soft on communism', bullying witnesses at hearings, and using the press to spread his claims. From 1953 he chaired a Senate investigations subcommittee. People feared that if they criticised him they would be accused next.

Opposition grew. In June 1950 Senator Margaret Chase Smith made her 'Declaration of Conscience' speech against his tactics. In March 1954 journalist Edward R. Murrow's television programme See It Now exposed McCarthy's methods.

evidence: June 1950: Margaret Chase Smith's 'Declaration of Conscience'.

sections.title: 3. McCarthy's downfall and the impact of McCarthyism

blocks.p: McCarthy went too far when he accused the US Army of hiding communists. The Army–McCarthy hearings (April–June 1954) were shown on television to millions. Viewers saw him bully witnesses; the Army's lawyer Joseph Welch asked, 'Have you no sense of decency, sir?' His popularity collapsed. In December 1954 the Senate voted to censure him. He died in 1957.

Impact: thousands lost their jobs; blacklists damaged careers in film, education and government; loyalty oaths spread; people were afraid to express opinions or join organisations, and free speech suffered. It also made anti-communism a central part of US politics for decades.

flashcards.q: Give three Cold War reasons for the Red Scare.
flashcards.a: Soviet control of Eastern Europe; Soviet atomic bomb 1949; communist China 1949; Korean War 1950.
The House Un-American Activities Committee, which investigated suspected communists, including in Hollywood.
Accusations without evidence; changing numbers; bullying witnesses; smearing opponents; using the press.

flashcards.q: Give two reasons for McCarthy's downfall.
flashcards.a: He attacked the army; televised hearings exposed him; Murrow's programme; Senate censure.
Lost jobs and blacklists; loyalty oaths; fear and conformity; anti-communism central to politics.
